title: Job 34:16–30
context: Elihu goes on to argue that the ruler of the world must be just. God shows no partiality to princes or the rich, sees every human way, removes the mighty, and hears the cry of the poor. His description of God’s just rule is shared ground between the traditions; whether it fits Job’s case, which the prologue explains differently, is part of the wider debate about Elihu.

verses.text: “If now you have understanding, hear this. Listen to the voice of my words.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu calls Job to hear and listen if he has understanding. He addresses Job directly.

Arminian readers note that Elihu presents his argument as an appeal to reason and invites Job to weigh it.
verses.reformedNotes:
The shift to address Job personally opens a sustained argument about God’s just rule.

Reformed readers see Elihu pressing his case. Both traditions read this as shared ground and continue to report Elihu’s words without declaring a verdict on his standing in the book.

verses.text: Should even one who hates justice govern? Will you condemn him who is righteous and mighty,
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu asks whether one who hates justice could govern, and whether Job will condemn the righteous and mighty one. He argues from God’s rule.

Arminian readers affirm that the world’s ruler must be just.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elihu implies that Job’s complaints amount to condemning God, a reading of Job that interpreters assess differently.

Reformed readers affirm God’s righteous rule. Both traditions read the principle as shared ground while weighing its application to Job.

verses.text: who says to a king, ‘Vile!’ or to nobles, ‘Wicked!’?
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu describes God as one who says to a king, ‘Vile!’ and to nobles, ‘Wicked!’ No ruler is beyond his judgment.

Arminian readers affirm that God holds the powerful accountable.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse is often read as describing God’s impartial authority over rulers, though some take it as a rhetorical question about human courts.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty over all authority. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: He doesn’t respect the persons of princes, nor respect the rich more than the poor, for they all are the work of his hands.
verses.arminianNotes:
God does not show partiality to princes or favor the rich over the poor, for all are the work of his hands. Impartiality follows from creation.

Arminian readers affirm God’s equal regard for all people.
verses.reformedNotes:
The ground of impartiality is that all are God’s creatures, a theme found elsewhere in biblical wisdom.

Reformed readers affirm God’s impartial justice. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about God’s fairness toward rich and poor alike.

verses.text: In a moment they die, even at midnight. The people are shaken and pass away. The mighty are taken away without a hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu says rulers die in a moment, even at midnight; the mighty are removed without human hand. Power is fragile.

Arminian readers see the brevity of human power before God, who can remove the mighty at any time.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘without a hand’ suggests removal by God rather than by human agency, though the phrase is brief.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereign rule over rulers. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the fragility of human power and God’s authority over it.

verses.text: “For his eyes are on the ways of a man. He sees all his goings.
verses.arminianNotes:
God’s eyes are on a person’s ways, and he sees all his steps. Nothing escapes him.

Arminian readers affirm God’s full knowledge of human conduct, which Job himself does not deny (compare 10:4–7).
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse begins a section on God’s knowledge as the basis of his judgment.

Reformed readers affirm God’s omniscience. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about God’s complete knowledge of every human life and every action.

verses.text: There is no darkness, nor thick gloom, where the workers of iniquity may hide themselves.
verses.arminianNotes:
No darkness or deep shadow can hide evildoers from God. Concealment is impossible.

Arminian readers affirm that God sees the wicked wherever they are, a truth Scripture affirms in many places.
verses.reformedNotes:
The image of darkness unable to hide recalls Psalm 139, though without direct quotation.

Reformed readers likewise affirm God’s all-seeing presence. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s knowledge and the impossibility of hiding from him.

verses.text: For he doesn’t need to consider a man further, that he should go before God in judgment.
verses.arminianNotes:
Elihu says God does not need to examine a person further before bringing him to judgment. God’s knowledge is complete.

Arminian readers note that this answers Job’s wish for a hearing with God.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse may respond to Job’s desire to present his case before God (23:3), though Elihu does not quote him directly. Its exact sense is debated.

Reformed readers see God needing no investigation. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: He breaks mighty men in pieces in ways past finding out, and sets others in their place.
verses.arminianNotes:
God breaks the mighty in ways past finding out and sets others in their place. History is under his hand.

Arminian readers see God’s rule over the rise and fall of the powerful, carried out in ways beyond human tracing.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘past finding out’ stresses the mystery of God’s ways.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereign governance of history. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s authority over rulers, without claiming to trace each instance of it.

verses.text: Therefore he takes knowledge of their works. He overturns them in the night, so that they are destroyed.
verses.arminianNotes:
God knows their works and overturns them in the night, so they are destroyed. Judgment comes suddenly.

Arminian readers affirm God’s just response to the deeds of the wicked, whose works he fully knows.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elihu continues to describe God’s judgment of the powerful. The pattern he describes is general, not a claim that every suffering is judgment.

Reformed readers see God’s justice at work. Both traditions read this as shared ground, remembering that the prologue explains Job’s case differently.

verses.text: He strikes them as wicked men in the open sight of others;
verses.arminianNotes:
God strikes them as wicked men in the open sight of others. Judgment is public.

Arminian readers see God’s justice made visible so that others may learn from it and turn from evil.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elihu presents public judgment as a lesson to onlookers.

Reformed readers see God’s justice displayed openly. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s judgment of the wicked, without applying it to Job’s particular case, where the book shows a different cause.

verses.text: because they turned away from following him, and wouldn’t pay attention to any of his ways,
verses.arminianNotes:
They are judged because they turned from following God and ignored his ways. The cause is their rebellion.

Arminian readers see judgment following a deliberate choice to turn from God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Elihu grounds judgment in moral rebellion, not in arbitrary power.

Reformed readers see sin’s consequences under God’s justice. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the link between turning from God and judgment, as Elihu describes the wicked.

verses.text: so that they caused the cry of the poor to come to him. He heard the cry of the afflicted.
verses.arminianNotes:
Their oppression caused the cry of the poor to reach God, and he heard the cry of the afflicted. God hears the oppressed.

Arminian readers affirm God’s compassion for the poor and afflicted.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse joins God’s judgment of oppressors with his care for their victims.

Reformed readers see God as defender of the afflicted. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about God’s attentiveness to the cry of the poor and his justice toward their oppressors.

verses.text: When he gives quietness, who then can condemn? When he hides his face, who then can see him? He is over a nation or a man alike,
verses.arminianNotes:
When God gives quietness, who can condemn; when he hides his face, who can see him? He rules over nation and person alike. God’s freedom is affirmed.

Arminian readers see God’s rule beyond human challenge.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse may touch Job’s experience of God’s hiddenness, though Elihu does not say so. Its sense is compact.

Reformed readers affirm God’s sovereignty over peace and trouble. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: that the godless man may not reign, that there be no one to ensnare the people.
verses.arminianNotes:
God acts so that the godless may not reign and ensnare the people. His rule protects.

Arminian readers see God’s governance aimed at the good of the people, guarding them from oppressive rulers.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse and the preceding one are difficult, and translations vary in detail.

Reformed readers see God’s providence restraining wicked rulers. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s care for his people in governing the world, while holding the exact sense tentatively.
